purpose: Implement a backward-compatible versioned password hashing scheme in source code, as the owner authorised, removing the silent truncation bcrypt applies at 72 bytes. Not a production deploy and not a bulk migration. New and changed passwords are written with scrypt from node:crypto; legacy bcrypt hashes keep verifying so no active user is locked out.
requiredInvariants: No database schema change. passwordHash is a plain string column, so changing the hash FORMAT touches no schema; this was checked rather than assumed, and it is what separates this item from V6.5.1 (#4682) where durable state would have required a column.
No new dependency. scrypt comes from node:crypto, so no licence, provenance, SBOM or vulnerability review is opened.

No invented cryptography. The scheme is scrypt with an explicit algorithm, version and parameter marker in the stored string; parsing fails closed on any unknown scheme, unknown version, non-numeric parameter, N that is not a power of two, malformed base64 or missing field.
Existing bcrypt hashes keep verifying. No active user is locked out, no forced reset, and no hash is ever rewritten without a password having been presented and verified.

The scrypt parameters were chosen by measuring against the bcrypt cost in use (338.8 ms versus 350.0 ms on the target stack), not from memory. Comparable work is mandatory here rather than cosmetic: DUMMY_PASSWORD_HASH stays bcrypt, and a cost divergence between the two login branches would reopen the timing oracle this module was written to close.

The existing timing-oracle suite is preserved, not weakened. One assertion that phrased the property as 'the same bcrypt rounds' is restated as the parameter pair it was measured against, because a stored password is no longer bcrypt; the intent is unchanged and still enforceable.

No wall-clock assertion is added to CI. The existing file explains that timing on shared runners is unstable and does not explain a failure; parameters are asserted instead, exactly as bcrypt's cost already is.

V6.2.8 deliberately stays FAIL. A legacy account still verifies through bcrypt and still truncates, so the requirement is not met for that population; claiming PASS on a working implementation that is not yet universally in force would be exactly the error this programme exists to avoid.
No production rollout, migration evidence or rollback plan is claimed. Production acceptance remains a separate, open item under separate authority.
apps/landing is not touched. No production, REG.RU, DNS, database or credential mutation.

Two existing specs asserted the stored hash was bcrypt and had to be restated, not deleted: password-hashing.spec.ts's equal-cost assertion, and gekta-registration.spec.ts's bcrypt.compare on the stored value. Both now assert the property that still matters - the stored value is a hash of that password, written under the measured-equivalent scheme - through the module's own verifier rather than a named algorithm. Every remaining bcrypt.getRounds assertion targets DUMMY_PASSWORD_HASH or comparisonHashFor(absent), which stay bcrypt by design and are untouched.
acceptance: A password longer than 72 bytes is distinguished from one sharing its first 72 bytes, in ASCII and in Cyrillic, and the same pair is shown to collide under the old scheme so the change is demonstrated rather than asserted.
Legacy bcrypt hashes still verify, including the older $2a$ prefix.
Malformed, unknown-scheme and unknown-version records are refused and are never rehashed.
verifyPasswordWithUpgrade verifies before computing, passes the previous value as a precondition for a compare-and-set, and a failed write leaves the login valid and the old hash intact.
Restoring the truncating bcrypt scheme fails 8 of the 40 cases across both suites.
The matrix rebuilds at applied 332 / rejected 0 with no verdict moved: V6.2.8 remains FAIL with a rewritten, self-revoking condition naming what is left.
